name: FaceTite / Renuvion

lead: These devices tighten loose skin along the jawline, jowls and neck without a facelift. FaceTite places a small probe under the skin that delivers bipolar radiofrequency energy; Renuvion uses helium plasma with radiofrequency energy to heat and contract subdermal tissue.

Heat contracts tissue and stimulates collagen remodeling, giving a tighter jaw-neck line. Surgeons describe them for patients with laxity too much for noninvasive devices but not enough to justify excisional surgery, sometimes combined with liposuction. Published evidence is mostly retrospective reviews and case series; no randomized trials were found.

paras: Energy is delivered through small access points, often combined with liposuction or fractional radiofrequency. Results develop over the weeks after treatment as tissue contracts.

Described complications include superficial burns, seromas, asymmetry and pigmentation changes, with rarer infection, nerve damage and scarring. The FDA has cleared Renuvion for specific indications and warned against off-label use. A 2026 paper discusses fibrosis and fat loss complicating later neck lift surgery.

angle.text: A tighter jawline and neck without a facelift. Heat applied under the skin makes tissue contract and remodel, tightening loose skin over the following weeks. Evidence is mostly case series, and the FDA has warned about off-label use.

lead: FaceTite and Renuvion are minimally invasive devices for tightening loose skin and contouring the lower face and neck. FaceTite, from InMode, delivers bipolar radiofrequency energy to the subdermal space through a small probe; Renuvion, which grew out of the J-Plasma system from Apyx Medical (formerly Bovie Medical), uses helium plasma energy to heat and contract subdermal soft tissue.[1][2][3]

Their appeal for appearance is a sharper jawline, tighter jowls and a leaner submental area without the scars and downtime of a facelift or neck lift. They are discussed as options in what surgeons call the treatment gap: patients with laxity too severe for traditional noninvasive devices but not severe enough to justify an excisional operation.[4][3] Both are often combined with liposuction and, in some practices, buccal fat pad excision.[5]

Published studies are largely retrospective reviews and descriptive case series, often reporting surgeon assessments of photographs, and a 2025 systematic review of Renuvion found 25 publications with usable patient data and noted the lack of standardized measured comparisons.[6] Complications such as burns and the FDA's warnings about off-label Renuvion use are part of the picture.[2]
infobox: Dermal resurfacing (May 2022); lax skin of the neck (July 2022); subcutaneous tissue contraction (Feb 2023)
Retrospective series for the face; some randomized trials in other body areas

paras: A 2022 review of subcutaneous radiofrequency-assisted liposculpture states that FaceTite and the related AccuTite can deliver energy into the subdermal space to target dermal collagen, offering an option for skin laxity and excess adipose of the face and neck with less downtime, lower cost and fewer complications than neck lift or face and neck lift.[1] Radiofrequency-based minimally invasive systems such as BodyTite, FaceTite and AccuTite are described by one surgeon as procedures for fat destruction and skin tightening, used alongside devices such as Morpheus8 and VASERlipo.[7]

Renuvion combines helium plasma with radiofrequency to heat and contract tissue.[2] A 2019 review describes the device as instantly heating tissue to above 85 degrees Celsius for between 0.040 and 0.080 seconds, with surrounding tissue staying cooler and cooling rapidly by conduction, which the authors say lowers the risk of injury compared with bulk-heating devices.[8] The same family of devices has been used for helium-plasma skin resurfacing, where one review describes pulsed and fractionated techniques,[9] and as an energy tool during rhytidectomy, where energy devices are described as offering better hemostasis and late 'shrink-wrap' collagen effects.[10]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports FDA clearances for the J-Plasma generator in 2009 and for expanded indications including dermal resurfacing in May 2022, improving the appearance of lax skin in the neck in July 2022, and coagulating and contracting subcutaneous soft tissue in February 2023.[2] The 2025 systematic review states that Renuvion recently received 501(k) clearance for soft tissue contraction after liposuction.[6]

sections.h: How the procedures are meant to change the face and neck
paras: Both technologies target the lower face and neck, where loose skin and a soft submental area blur the jaw and neck angle. The intended chain is: energy is delivered under the skin, collagen contracts and the tissue tightens over the following weeks and months, and the jawline and neck look more defined. With FaceTite, a 2022 review describes energy delivered into the subdermal space to target dermal collagen, with surgeons using it for laxity and excess fat of the face and neck as an option with less downtime, lower cost and fewer complications than a neck lift.[1] With Renuvion, helium plasma and radiofrequency are used to heat and contract tissue; a 2019 review says tissue is heated above 85 degrees Celsius for between 0.040 and 0.080 seconds while surrounding tissue cools quickly, which the authors say lowers the risk of injury compared with bulk-heating devices.[2][8]

Surgeons also use the energy during or after liposuction. A 2024 paper describes radiofrequency-assisted neck liposuction with FaceTite combined with buccal fat pad excision for slimming and sculpting of the neck and jawline, which is the combination that most directly connects the devices to the lean-face aesthetic discussed in jawline communities.[5]

The procedures are placed in the hardmaxxing category of jawline and neck refinement as a lower-downtime alternative to surgery for jowls and a soft submental area. They sit beside facelift, neck lift, buccal fat removal and liposuction as options for a more defined lower face.[5][11]

A 2019 paper describes combining adjustable-depth fractional radiofrequency with bipolar radiofrequency as a minimally invasive treatment for skin laxity.[4] A retrospective review published in 2020 evaluated the combination of FaceTite with fractional bipolar RF for lower face and neck laxity and describes itself as the largest evaluation to date of that combination.[3]
A 2024 paper describes integrating neck liposuction using FaceTite radiofrequency with buccal fat pad excision for facial slimming and sculpting of the neck and jawline.[5]

The US Food and Drug Administration has addressed Renuvion in a series of safety communications. In its May 2023 update, the agency listed the cleared indications: the Renuvion APR handpiece (cleared April 27, 2023) for coagulation of subcutaneous tissue after liposuction for body contouring, coagulation and contraction of soft tissue, improving the appearance of loose skin in the neck and submental region, and open-surgery cutting, coagulation and ablation; and the Renuvion Dermal handpiece (cleared May 2022) for moderate to severe wrinkles in Fitzpatrick skin types I to III only.[12] The FDA stated that dermal resurfacing or skin contraction with the general surgical handpieces is not cleared, a warning it first issued in March 2022, and that uses of the APR handpiece beyond its listed indications are also not cleared.[12]

The agency's recommendations to patients are to discuss the benefits and risks of the available aesthetic skin procedures with their provider and ask which devices will be used; for providers, it recommends reviewing risks and benefits, naming the device to patients and following the instructions for use and training, and it said it would continue monitoring adverse event reports.[12]

Grokipedia reports that superficial burns, seromas, asymmetry and pigmentation changes are the most common Renuvion complications, with infection, nerve damage, subcutaneous emphysema and scarring rarer, and that the FDA warned against off-label use for procedures such as skin resurfacing and full-body tightening where the device lacks clearance. It cites 135 adverse event reports between April 2020 and November 2023 including serious burns and bleeding.[2] Because the source is AI-generated, these figures should be checked against FDA documents.
A 2026 paper in Aesthetic Surgery Journal examined neck lift after nonsurgical treatments, describing fibrosis, fat loss and increased surgical complexity.[11]

A retrospective review of helium-based plasma technology for soft tissue coagulation examined its safety in practice.[13] The 2025 systematic review noted that most published studies relied on subjective evaluations and did not provide standardized photographs with measurements comparing Renuvion to traditional methods.[6]

Published facial data are mostly retrospective reviews and case series. They include a 2019 paper on combined fractional and bipolar radiofrequency for skin laxity,[4] a 2020 retrospective review of multimodal radiofrequency in lower face and neck laxity,[3] a 2022 review of subcutaneous radiofrequency-assisted liposculpture in facial plastic surgery practice,[1] and a 2024 report on FaceTite with buccal fat pad excision.[5] A small registered study examined radiofrequency for premature jowl and neck laxity after a facelift (NCT03945422, 11 participants).[14] No randomized controlled trials of FaceTite or Renuvion for the face were found.

Randomized studies exist for other body areas. One compared radiofrequency-assisted liposuction and Renuvion helium subdermal coagulation with a VASER-assisted control group for arm contouring,[15] and a prospective randomized study examined Renuvion for loose skin in patients undergoing abdominoplasty after massive weight loss.[16] The 2025 systematic review covered treatment areas including the face, neck, breasts, trunk and extremities, usually combined with liposuction.[6]

Reviewers describe the literature as mostly small and subjective. The 2025 systematic review reported that most published studies relied on subjective evaluations and lacked standardised photographs with measurements,[6] while the 2020 multimodal radiofrequency series for lower face and neck laxity described itself as the largest evaluation of the FaceTite and fractional bipolar combination, being a retrospective review of patients treated in practice.[3][3]

timeline.event: J-Plasma generator receives FDA clearance, per Grokipedia.[2]
Papers describe combined fractional and bipolar radiofrequency and Renuvion for subdermal tightening of the face and neck.[4][8]
FDA clearances for Renuvion dermal resurfacing (May) and lax neck skin (July), per Grokipedia.[2]
Clearance for coagulating and contracting subcutaneous soft tissue (February), per Grokipedia.[2]
